claim: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is an enzyme co-factor in eukaryotes.
source: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is an enzyme co-factor in eukaryotes that also plays a critical role in protecting photosynthetic eukaryotes against damaging reactive oxygen species derived from the chloroplast.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Ascorbic acid plays a critical role in protecting photosynthetic eukaryotes against damaging reactive oxygen species derived from the chloroplast.
source: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is an enzyme co-factor in eukaryotes that also plays a critical role in protecting photosynthetic eukaryotes against damaging reactive oxygen species derived from the chloroplast.
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations and experimental evidence discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Many animal lineages have become ascorbate auxotrophs due to the loss of the terminal enzyme in their biosynthetic pathway, l-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO).
source: Many animal lineages, including primates, have become ascorbate auxotrophs due to the loss of the terminal enzyme in their biosynthetic pathway, l-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on GULO loss in animals.

claim: The alternative pathways found in land plants and Euglena use a different terminal enzyme, l-galactonolactone dehydrogenase (GLDH).
source: The alternative pathways found in land plants and Euglena use a different terminal enzyme, l-galactonolactone dehydrogenase (GLDH).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: GULO was functionally replaced with GLDH in photosynthetic eukaryote lineages following plastid acquisition.
source: Here we present molecular and biochemical evidence demonstrating that GULO was functionally replaced with GLDH in photosynthetic eukaryote lineages following plastid acquisition.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by molecular and biochemical data presented in the results section.

claim: GULO has been lost repeatedly throughout eukaryote evolution.
source: GULO has therefore been lost repeatedly throughout eukaryote evolution.
evidence: This is supported by the genomic analysis showing absence of GULO in multiple lineages.

claim: The formation of alternative biosynthetic pathways in photosynthetic eukaryotes uncoupled ascorbate synthesis from hydrogen peroxide production.
source: The formation of the alternative biosynthetic pathways in photosynthetic eukaryotes uncoupled ascorbate synthesis from hydrogen peroxide production and likely contributed to the rise of ascorbate as a major photoprotective antioxidant.
evidence: This is based on the biochemical properties of GULO vs GLDH and their different electron acceptors.

claim: The majority of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) generated in some organelles is likely reduced by other antioxidant systems, such as the peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases in the mitochondria, and catalases in the peroxisome.
source: The majority of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) generated in some organelles is likely reduced by other antioxidant systems, such as the peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases in the mitochondria, and catalases in the peroxisome (Mhamdi et al., 2012; Sies, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ascorbate plays an important role in protecting photosynthetic cells against ROS derived from the chloroplast.
source: However, ascorbate plays an important role in protecting photosynthetic cells against ROS derived from the chloroplast (Smirnoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Ascorbate peroxidase (APX) is found in both the cytosol and the chloroplast of photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: Ascorbate peroxidase (APX), which is found in both the cytosol and the chloroplast of photosynthetic eukaryotes, is central to this photoprotective role.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APX localization.

claim: Thylakoid- and stroma-localised APX removes H2O2 produced by photosystem I through the activity of the ascorbate-glutathione cycle.
source: Thylakoid- and stroma-localised APX removes H2O2 produced by photosystem I through the activity of the ascorbate-glutathione cycle and this process may account for 10% of photosynthetic electron transport flow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ascorbate-glutathione cycle.

claim: The ascorbate-glutathione cycle may account for 10% of photosynthetic electron transport flow.
source: Thylakoid- and stroma-localised APX removes H2O2 produced by photosystem I through the activity of the ascorbate-glutathione cycle and this process may account for 10% of photosynthetic electron transport flow.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on previous research.

claim: Ascorbate plays a critical role in preventing lipid peroxidation in the thylakoid membranes.
source: Ascorbate also plays a critical role in preventing lipid peroxidation in the thylakoid membranes and acts as a co-factor for violaxanthin de-epoxidase in the xanthophyll cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ascorbate function.

claim: Ascorbate acts as a co-factor for violaxanthin de-epoxidase in the xanthophyll cycle.
source: Ascorbate also plays a critical role in preventing lipid peroxidation in the thylakoid membranes and acts as a co-factor for violaxanthin de-epoxidase in the xanthophyll cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the xanthophyll cycle.

claim: Ascorbate in the thylakoid lumen may prevent photoinhibition in high light by directly donating electrons to the photosynthetic electron transport chain.
source: In addition, ascorbate in the thylakoid lumen may prevent photoinhibition in high light by directly donating electrons to the photosynthetic electron transport chain (Smirnoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Ascorbate deficient plants display sensitivity to high light and to oxidants.
source: These roles have been demonstrated in a range of ascorbate deficient plants that display sensitivity to high light and to oxidants (Smirnoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article summarizing experimental evidence.

claim: Photosynthetic eukaryotes arose following the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote in the Archaeplastida (Plantae) lineage.
source: Photosynthetic eukaryotes arose following the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote in the Archaeplastida (Plantae) lineage (Keeling, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of photosynthetic eukaryotes, supported by citation.

claim: Several eukaryote lineages, including the diatoms, haptophytes and euglenids, gained plastids through a secondary endosymbiosis with either a red or green alga.
source: Several other eukaryote lineages, including the diatoms, haptophytes and euglenids, subsequently gained plastids through a secondary endosymbiosis with either a red or green alga.
evidence: This is established knowledge about secondary endosymbiosis.

claim: Plastid endosymbioses were accompanied by lateral gene transfer on a massive scale from the symbiont to the host nuclear genome (endosymbiotic gene transfer or EGT).
source: These plastid endosymbioses were accompanied by lateral gene transfer on a massive scale from the symbiont to the host nuclear genome (known as endosymbiotic gene transfer or EGT), giving rise to the complex physiologies of photosynthetic eukaryotes (Timmis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on EGT.

claim: The plastids in the major photosynthetic eukaryote lineages are all ultimately derived from the primary endosymbiosis.
source: The plastids in the major photosynthetic eukaryote lineages are all ultimately derived from the primary endosymbiosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plastid evolution.

claim: The plastid is a major source of potentially damaging ROS.
source: Whilst acquisition of a photosynthetic endosymbiont may have been beneficial to the host cell in many ways, the plastid is also a major source of potentially damaging ROS (Dorrell and Howe, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is evidence for extensive leakage of H2O2 out of plastids via aquaporins, particularly at high light intensities.
source: There is evidence for extensive leakage of H2O2 out of plastids via aquaporins, particularly at high light intensities (Mubarakshina et al., 2010; Naydov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plastid acquisition is associated with a greatly increased requirement for cellular antioxidant systems to prevent photodamage.
source: Plastid acquisition is therefore associated with a greatly increased requirement for cellular antioxidant systems to prevent photodamage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased ROS production from plastids.

claim: Cyanobacteria do not possess APX or any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis.
source: Cyanobacteria do not possess APX or any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis and minimise photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases (Zámocký et al., 2010; Gest et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cyanobacteria minimise photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases.
source: Cyanobacteria do not possess APX or any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis and minimise photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases (Zámocký et al., 2010; Gest et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ascorbate was most likely recruited to its photoprotective role after the acquisition of the plastid in ancestral Archaeplastida.
source: This suggests that ascorbate was most likely recruited to its photoprotective role after the acquisition of the plastid in ancestral Archaeplastida (Gest et al., 2013), although the evolutionary origins of ascorbate biosynthesis are unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ascorbate biosynthesis in cyanobacteria, supported by citation.

claim: There is no clear evidence for ascorbate biosynthesis in prokaryotes.
source: There is no clear evidence for ascorbate biosynthesis in prokaryotes (see 'Materials and methods'), suggesting that the ability to synthesise ascorbate evolved in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is based on extensive sequence searches and literature review discussed in Materials and methods.

claim: The ability to synthesise ascorbate evolved in eukaryotes.
source: There is no clear evidence for ascorbate biosynthesis in prokaryotes (see 'Materials and methods'), suggesting that the ability to synthesise ascorbate evolved in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ascorbate biosynthesis in prokaryotes.

claim: The three eukaryote lineages in which ascorbate biosynthesis has been examined extensively (animals, plants and Euglena) all exhibit different biosynthetic pathways.
source: The three eukaryote lineages in which ascorbate biosynthesis has been examined extensively (animals, plants and Euglena) all exhibit different biosynthetic pathways (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical evidence and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Animals synthesise ascorbate via D-glucuronic acid and l-gulonolactone (l-GulL), with l-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO) catalysing the oxidation of l-GulL to ascorbate.
source: Animals synthesise ascorbate via D-glucuronic acid and l-gulonolactone (l-GulL), with l-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO) catalysing the oxidation of l-GulL to ascorbate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the animal pathway.

claim: In all of the animal ascorbate auxotrophs that have been examined, the gene encoding GULO is lost.
source: In all of the animal ascorbate auxotrophs that have been examined, the gene encoding GULO is lost (Nishikimi et al., 1992, 1994; Cui et al., 2011a; Drouin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GULO uses molecular O2 as its electron acceptor, resulting in H2O2 production.
source: GULO uses molecular O2 as its electron acceptor, resulting in H2O2 production, which may have contributed to selective pressure to lose this enzyme in some animals (Bánhegyi et al., 1996; Mandl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GULO biochemistry, supported by citations.

claim: H2O2 production by GULO may have contributed to selective pressure to lose this enzyme in some animals.
source: GULO uses molecular O2 as its electron acceptor, resulting in H2O2 production, which may have contributed to selective pressure to lose this enzyme in some animals (Bánhegyi et al., 1996; Mandl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two alternative routes to ascorbate biosynthesis have been identified in photosynthetic eukaryotes, which both employ l-galactonolactone dehydrogenase (GLDH) as the terminal enzyme instead of GULO.
source: Two alternative routes to ascorbate biosynthesis have been identified in photosynthetic eukaryotes, which both employ l-galactonolactone dehydrogenase (GLDH) as the terminal enzyme instead of GULO.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on biochemical studies.

claim: A pathway via D-galacturonic acid and l-galactonolactone (l-GalL) was identified in Euglena.
source: A pathway via D-galacturonic acid and l-galactonolactone (l-GalL) was identified in Euglena (Shigeoka et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The euglenid pathway appears to be functional in some stramenopile algae.
source: This pathway is analogous to the animal pathway and also appears to be functional in some stramenopile algae (Helsper et al., 1982; Grün and Loewus, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ascorbate biosynthesis in land plants occurs via a route using D-mannose and l-galactose.
source: In contrast, ascorbate biosynthesis in land plants was found to occur via a different route using D-mannose and l-galactose (Wheeler et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Green algae use the 'plant pathway'.
source: Green algae also use the 'plant pathway' (Running et al., 2003; Urzica et al., 2012), but evidence is lacking for the nature of ascorbate biosynthesis in many other evolutionarily important lineages, most notably the rhodophytes (red algae).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GULO and GLDH exhibit significant sequence similarity and are both members of the vanillyl alcohol oxidase (VAO) family of flavoproteins.
source: GULO and GLDH exhibit significant sequence similarity and are both members of the vanillyl alcohol oxidase (VAO) family of flavoproteins (Leferink et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GULO can oxidise l-GulL and l-GalL, whereas GLDH is highly specific for l-GalL.
source: GULO can oxidise l-GulL and l-GalL, whereas GLDH is highly specific for l-GalL (Smirnoff, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GULO localises to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: GULO localises to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), whereas GLDH is associated with complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain (Schertl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GLDH is associated with complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
source: GULO localises to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), whereas GLDH is associated with complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain (Schertl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GLDH does not generate H2O2, as it uses cytochrome c rather than O2 as an electron acceptor.
source: Importantly, GLDH does not generate H2O2, as it uses cytochrome c rather than O2 as an electron acceptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GLDH biochemistry.

claim: GULO and GLDH have a mutually exclusive distribution in eukaryote genomes.
source: We found that GULO and GLDH have a mutually exclusive distribution (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis presented in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: GULO is absent from many metazoan genomes, including all insects.
source: GULO is absent from many metazoan genomes, including all insects, supporting earlier biochemical evidence that insects are predominately ascorbate auxotrophs (Supplementary file 1) (Chatterjee, 1973; Dadd, 1973).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GULO is present in basally derived metazoans, including sponges and cnidarians.
source: However, GULO is present in basally derived metazoans, including sponges and cnidarians, and is also present in a filasterean (Capsaspora owczarzaki) and in fungi (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GULO is present in a filasterean (Capsaspora owczarzaki) and in fungi.
source: However, GULO is present in basally derived metazoans, including sponges and cnidarians, and is also present in a filasterean (Capsaspora owczarzaki) and in fungi (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Ascorbate synthesis via GULO is an ancestral trait in the Opisthokonta that has been lost in many lineages.
source: This suggests that ascorbate synthesis via GULO is an ancestral trait in the Opisthokonta that has been lost in many lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of GULO in basally derived lineages.

claim: GULO is present in the Apusomonadida (Thecamonas trahens), a sister group to the Opisthokonts.
source: GULO is also present the Apusomonadida (Thecamonas trahens), a sister group to the Opisthokonts, and in members of the Amoebozoa and Excavata.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GULO is present in members of the Amoebozoa and Excavata.
source: GULO is also present the Apusomonadida (Thecamonas trahens), a sister group to the Opisthokonts, and in members of the Amoebozoa and Excavata.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GULO is present in basally derived Archaeplastida including the glaucophyte, Cyanophora paradoxa, and the rhodophytes Galdieria sulphuraria and Galdieria phlegrea.
source: Surprisingly, we also found GULO in basally derived Archaeplastida including the glaucophyte, Cyanophora paradoxa, and the rhodophytes Galdieria sulphuraria and Galdieria phlegrea.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: The glaucophytes occupy a key position in the evolution of photosynthetic eukaryotes as they diverged from the other Archaeplastida before the split of the red and green algal lineages.
source: The glaucophytes occupy a key position in the evolution of photosynthetic eukaryotes as they diverged from the other Archaeplastida before the split of the red and green algal lineages and have highly unusual chloroplasts (termed cyanelles) that retain several features of the cyanobacterial endosymbiont (Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glaucophyte evolution, supported by citation.

claim: Glaucophytes have highly unusual chloroplasts (termed cyanelles) that retain several features of the cyanobacterial endosymbiont.
source: The glaucophytes occupy a key position in the evolution of photosynthetic eukaryotes as they diverged from the other Archaeplastida before the split of the red and green algal lineages and have highly unusual chloroplasts (termed cyanelles) that retain several features of the cyanobacterial endosymbiont (Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glaucophyte chloroplasts, supported by citation.

claim: GULO is absent from all other Archaeplastida genomes.
source: GULO is absent from all other Archaeplastida genomes, although an enzyme family exhibiting weak similarity to GULO has been reported in Arabidopsis (Maruta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GLDH was found in all Archaeplastida genomes, except for Cyanophora and Galdieria.
source: GLDH was found in all Archaeplastida genomes, except for Cyanophora and Galdieria, and in all photosynthetic lineages that have acquired a plastid via secondary endosymbiosis (including stramenopiles, cryptophytes, haptophytes, chlorarachniophytes and euglenids).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GLDH is found in all photosynthetic lineages that have acquired a plastid via secondary endosymbiosis (including stramenopiles, cryptophytes, haptophytes, chlorarachniophytes and euglenids).
source: GLDH was found in all Archaeplastida genomes, except for Cyanophora and Galdieria, and in all photosynthetic lineages that have acquired a plastid via secondary endosymbiosis (including stramenopiles, cryptophytes, haptophytes, chlorarachniophytes and euglenids).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: GLDH was present in several non-photosynthetic organisms including the oomycetes, the foraminifera and in the choanoflagellates, Monosiga brevicollis and Salpingoeca rosetta.
source: GLDH was present in several non-photosynthetic organisms including the oomycetes, the foraminifera and in the choanoflagellates, Monosiga brevicollis and Salpingoeca rosetta.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Nearly all photosynthetic eukaryotes use GLDH rather than GULO as the terminal enzyme in ascorbate biosynthesis.
source: We conclude that nearly all photosynthetic eukaryotes use GLDH rather than GULO as the terminal enzyme in ascorbate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genomic analysis.

claim: The exceptions to photosynthetic eukaryotes using GLDH are the basally derived Archaeplastida (Cyanophora, Galdieria and Chlorokybus) and the chromerids.
source: The exceptions are the basally derived Archaeplastida (Cyanophora, Galdieria and Chlorokybus) and the chromerids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No photosynthetic organisms were found to lack both GULO and GLDH.
source: No photosynthetic organisms were found to lack both GULO and GLDH, although both genes were absent in many non-photosynthetic organisms, including all insects, Daphnia, Paramecium and Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Both GULO and GLDH are absent in many non-photosynthetic organisms, including all insects, Daphnia, Paramecium and Dictyostelium.
source: No photosynthetic organisms were found to lack both GULO and GLDH, although both genes were absent in many non-photosynthetic organisms, including all insects, Daphnia, Paramecium and Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Organisms lacking both GULO and GLDH are likely to be ascorbate auxotrophs.
source: Since all documented pathways of ascorbate biosynthesis require either GULO or GLDH, organisms lacking both of these enzymes are likely to be ascorbate auxotrophs (Chatterjee, 1973).
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for these enzymes in known pathways.

claim: GLDH is highly conserved and has a monophyletic origin for all GLDH sequences.
source: GLDH is highly conserved and the phylogenetic analyses strongly support a monophyletic origin for all GLDH sequences (100% bootstrap support, posterior probability = 1) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The monophyly of eukaryote GULO sequences is well supported (85% bootstrap support, posterior probability = 1).
source: The monophyly of eukaryote GULO sequences is well supported (85% bootstrap support, posterior probability = 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There is moderate support for the monophyly of GULO and GLDH as a clade within the VAO family.
source: There is also moderate support for the monophyly of GULO and GLDH as a clade within the VAO family, supporting hypotheses that these enzymes may have originated from a gene duplication event.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: GULO and GLDH may have originated from a gene duplication event.
source: There is also moderate support for the monophyly of GULO and GLDH as a clade within the VAO family, supporting hypotheses that these enzymes may have originated from a gene duplication event.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: GLDH is highly unusual amongst the VAO flavoprotein family in that it does not use O2 as an electron acceptor.
source: GLDH is highly unusual amongst the VAO flavoprotein family in that it does not use O2 as an electron acceptor, but mutation of a single highly conserved alanine residue in GLDH is required to convert it from a dehydrogenase to an oxidase (Leferink et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Mutation of a single highly conserved alanine residue in GLDH is required to convert it from a dehydrogenase to an oxidase.
source: GLDH is highly unusual amongst the VAO flavoprotein family in that it does not use O2 as an electron acceptor, but mutation of a single highly conserved alanine residue in GLDH is required to convert it from a dehydrogenase to an oxidase (Leferink et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: VTC2 is found exclusively in the Viridiplantae (including Chlorokybus).
source: VTC2 is found exclusively in the Viridiplantae (including Chlorokybus), indicating that the definitive 'plant' pathway is restricted to this lineage (Figure 2; Supplementary files 3, 4).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 2 and supplementary files.

claim: The definitive 'plant' pathway is restricted to the Viridiplantae lineage.
source: VTC2 is found exclusively in the Viridiplantae (including Chlorokybus), indicating that the definitive 'plant' pathway is restricted to this lineage (Figure 2; Supplementary files 3, 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of VTC2.

claim: Organisms that lack VTC2 but possess GLDH are likely to operate a 'euglenid' pathway, with D-galacturonic acid acting as the precursor of l-GalL.
source: Biochemical evidence from euglenids and stramenopiles (Shigeoka et al., 1979; Helsper et al., 1982; Grun and Loewus, 1984) suggests that organisms that lack VTC2 but possess GLDH are likely to operate a 'euglenid' pathway, with D-galacturonic acid acting as the precursor of l-GalL.
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical evidence from previous research.

claim: NAD+-dependent l-galactose dehydrogenase activity was detected in Porphyra thallus extracts.
source: We detected NAD+-dependent l-galactose dehydrogenase activity in Porphyra thallus extracts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Feeding 10 mM l-galactose to Porphyra thallus slices increased the concentration of ascorbate.
source: Feeding 10 mM l-galactose to Porphyra thallus slices increased the concentration of ascorbate (detected as dehydroascorbate by GC-MS) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rhodophytes likely use a modified 'plant pathway' to synthesise ascorbate, employing an unidentified enzyme activity to generate l-galactose from GDP-l-galactose instead of VTC2.
source: As red algae synthesise GDP-l-galactose from GDP-D-mannose (Su and Hassid, 1962), rhodophytes likely use a modified 'plant pathway' to synthesise ascorbate, employing an unidentified enzyme activity to generate l-galactose from GDP-l-galactose instead of VTC2.
evidence: This is an inference based on biochemical evidence and the presence of l-galactose dehydrogenase.

claim: l-galactose, l-GalL and l-GulL were all effective precursors of ascorbate in G. sulphuraria.
source: l-galactose, l-GalL and l-GulL were all effective precursors of ascorbate in G. sulphuraria (Figure 4C), suggesting that l-galactose is converted to l-GalL, which may then be converted to ascorbate by GULO.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In G. sulphuraria, l-galactose is converted to l-GalL, which may then be converted to ascorbate by GULO.
source: l-galactose, l-GalL and l-GulL were all effective precursors of ascorbate in G. sulphuraria (Figure 4C), suggesting that l-galactose is converted to l-GalL, which may then be converted to ascorbate by GULO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Positional isotopic labelling in G. sulphuraria indicated that label from D-[1-13C]-glucose was incorporated primarily into carbon 1 (C1) of ascorbate.
source: A positional isotopic labelling approach indicated that label from D-[1-13C]-glucose was incorporated primarily into carbon 1 (C1) of ascorbate (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The labelling pattern in G. sulphuraria is expected for the plant pathway, indicating non-inversion of the carbon chain.
source: This labelling pattern is expected for the plant pathway, while the reduction of a uronic acid intermediate in the animal or euglenid pathways would result in the transfer of label from C1 of glucose into C6 of ascorbate/dehydroascorbate (Loewus, 1999).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on established knowledge.

claim: G. sulphuraria uses a similar pathway to other rhodophytes, employing GULO instead of GLDH.
source: G. sulphuraria therefore uses a similar pathway to other rhodophytes, employing GULO instead of GLDH.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The Archaeplastida generate l-GalL via l-galactose (without inversion of the carbon chain of glucose).
source: The Archaeplastida generate l-GalL via l-galactose (without inversion of the carbon chain of glucose), whereas photosynthetic eukaryotes with secondary plastids synthesise l-GalL via D-galacturonate, resulting in inversion of the carbon chain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on biochemical evidence.

claim: Photosynthetic eukaryotes with secondary plastids synthesise l-GalL via D-galacturonate, resulting in inversion of the carbon chain.
source: The Archaeplastida generate l-GalL via l-galactose (without inversion of the carbon chain of glucose), whereas photosynthetic eukaryotes with secondary plastids synthesise l-GalL via D-galacturonate, resulting in inversion of the carbon chain.
evidence: This is based on biochemical evidence from previous research.

claim: APX and APX-R are found in nearly all photosynthetic eukaryotes and in the choanoflagellates, M. brevicollis and S. rosetta.
source: APX and APX-R are found in nearly all photosynthetic eukaryotes and in the choanoflagellates, M. brevicollis and S. rosetta.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Euglena and Emiliania do not possess APX or APX-R, although both possess APX-CCX.
source: Euglena and Emiliania do not possess APX or APX-R, although both possess APX-CCX, which is also found in some fungi and in Capsaspora (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The only photosynthetic eukaryote in this analysis that lacks any isoform of APX was C. paradoxa.
source: The only photosynthetic eukaryote in this analysis that lacks any isoform of APX was C. paradoxa.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Cyanophora lacks all of the remaining enzymes of the plant ascorbate-glutathione cycle: monodehydroascorbate reductase (MDHAR), dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) and glutathione reductase (GR).
source: Cyanophora also lacks all of the remaining enzymes of the plant ascorbate-glutathione cycle: monodehydroascorbate reductase (MDHAR), dehydroascorbate reductase (DHAR) and glutathione reductase (GR).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: The ascorbate-dependent xanthophyll cycle is not present in glaucophytes.
source: The ascorbate-dependent xanthophyll cycle is not present in glaucophytes and so Cyanophora does not require ascorbate for non-photochemical quenching (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ascorbate could not be detected in Cyanophora extracts using GC-MS.
source: Moreover, the cellular concentration of ascorbate in Cyanophora is either very low or absent, as we could not detect ascorbate in Cyanophora extracts using GC-MS (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Cyanophora is unlikely to rely on ascorbate to detoxify peroxides derived from photosynthesis.
source: However, in combination with the lack of the plant ascorbate-glutathione cycle and the xanthophyll cycle, we conclude that Cyanophora is unlikely to rely on ascorbate to detoxify peroxides derived from photosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genomic and biochemical data.

claim: Cyanophora contains several glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins and catalase, as well as a unique peroxidase (symerythrin) similar to rubrerythrin of prokaryotes.
source: Cyanophora does however contain several glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins and catalase, as well as a unique peroxidase (symerythrin) similar to rubrerythrin of prokaryotes (Cooley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and supported by citation.

claim: Glaucophytes rely on alternative mechanisms to detoxify peroxides derived from photosynthesis.
source: These data suggest that glaucophytes rely on alternative mechanisms to detoxify peroxides derived from photosynthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic and biochemical data.

claim: Cyanobacteria do not appear to use ascorbate for photoprotection.
source: As cyanobacteria also do not appear to use ascorbate for photoprotection (Bernroitner et al., 2009; Latifi et al., 2009), the photoprotective role of ascorbate may therefore have emerged in the Archaeplastida after the divergence of the glaucophytes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The photoprotective role of ascorbate may have emerged in the Archaeplastida after the divergence of the glaucophytes.
source: As cyanobacteria also do not appear to use ascorbate for photoprotection (Bernroitner et al., 2009; Latifi et al., 2009), the photoprotective role of ascorbate may therefore have emerged in the Archaeplastida after the divergence of the glaucophytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from Cyanophora and cyanobacteria.

claim: The distribution of GULO and GLDH in eukaryotes may be explained by either ancient paralogy followed by differential gene loss or EGT of GLDH followed by GULO loss.
source: In conclusion, the distribution of GULO and GLDH in eukaryotes may be explained by either of two evolutionary models; ancient paralogy followed by differential gene loss or EGT of GLDH followed by GULO loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: Both evolutionary models support GULO as an ancestral gene in the last common eukaryote ancestor.
source: However, they do enable clear conclusions to be made on the loss of GULO. Both evolutionary models support GULO as an ancestral gene in the last common eukaryote ancestor, indicating that GULO has been lost in almost all photosynthetic eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: GULO has been lost in almost all photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: Both evolutionary models support GULO as an ancestral gene in the last common eukaryote ancestor, indicating that GULO has been lost in almost all photosynthetic eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genomic analysis.

claim: Photosynthetic eukaryotes encountered strong selective pressure to replace the function of GULO in ascorbate biosynthesis.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that photosynthetic eukaryotes encountered strong selective pressure to replace the function of GULO in ascorbate biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: The critical role of ascorbate in photoprotection has been demonstrated in a diversity of photosynthetic eukaryotes, including land plants, green algae, diatoms and euglenids.
source: The critical role of ascorbate in photoprotection has been demonstrated in a diversity of photosynthetic eukaryotes, including land plants, green algae, diatoms and euglenids (Lavaud and Kroth, 2006; Ishikawa et al., 2010; Mellado et al., 2012; Urzica et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many photosynthetic eukaryotes possessed GULO prior to plastid acquisition.
source: Our analyses indicate that many photosynthetic eukaryotes possessed GULO prior to plastid acquisition, whereas almost all extant photosynthetic lineages use GLDH to synthesise ascorbate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis.

claim: Almost all extant photosynthetic lineages use GLDH to synthesise ascorbate.
source: Our analyses indicate that many photosynthetic eukaryotes possessed GULO prior to plastid acquisition, whereas almost all extant photosynthetic lineages use GLDH to synthesise ascorbate.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: The selective pressure to replace GULO in ascorbate biosynthesis following plastid acquisition could be linked to the photoprotective role of ascorbate.
source: The selective pressure to replace GULO in ascorbate biosynthesis following plastid acquisition could therefore be linked to the photoprotective role of ascorbate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: The production of H2O2 by GULO may have limited the ability of the host cell to protect itself against ROS derived from the chloroplast.
source: One intriguing possibility is that the production of H2O2 by GULO may have limited the ability of the host cell to protect itself against ROS derived from the chloroplast.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Ascorbate biosynthesis via GULO results in the production of H2O2 in the ER lumen.
source: However, ascorbate biosynthesis via GULO results in the production of H2O2 in the ER lumen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GULO biochemistry.

claim: In mammalian cells, ascorbate synthesis via GULO results in a damaging depletion and oxidation of the glutathione pool when ascorbate synthesis is increased by feeding l-GulL.
source: In mammalian cells, this results in a damaging depletion and oxidation of the glutathione pool when ascorbate synthesis is increased by feeding l-GulL (Bánhegyi et al., 1996; Puskás et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ancestral photosynthetic eukaryotes may have been unable to balance their increasing requirements for ascorbate biosynthesis with maintenance of the redox status within the ER.
source: Ancestral photosynthetic eukaryotes may have been unable to balance their increasing requirements for ascorbate biosynthesis with maintenance of the redox status within the ER, providing selective pressure to uncouple ascorbate biosynthesis from H2O2 production.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The presence of GULO rather than GLDH in the glaucophytes is consistent with the hypothesis that glaucophytes do not use ascorbate for photoprotection.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the presence of GULO rather than GLDH in the glaucophytes. As glaucophytes do not appear to use ascorbate for photoprotection, ascorbate biosynthesis would not have been subjected to the same selective pressures as other photosynthetic eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from Cyanophora.

claim: Galdieria is photosynthetic and expresses a functional APX.
source: Galdieria is photosynthetic and expresses a functional APX (Sano et al., 2001), but it is very sensitive to even moderate light intensities and grows primarily in an endolithic environment utilising heterotrophic carbon sources (Oesterhelt et al., 2007).

claim: Galdieria is very sensitive to even moderate light intensities and grows primarily in an endolithic environment utilising heterotrophic carbon sources.
source: Galdieria is photosynthetic and expresses a functional APX (Sano et al., 2001), but it is very sensitive to even moderate light intensities and grows primarily in an endolithic environment utilising heterotrophic carbon sources (Oesterhelt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Photo-oxidative stress in Galdieria's environment may be minimal, reducing the selective pressure to replace GULO.
source: Thus, photo-oxidative stress in this environment may be minimal, reducing the selective pressure in Galdieria to replace GULO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ecological characteristics of Galdieria.

claim: The selective pressures resulting in GULO loss in animals represent a combination of the costs of ascorbate synthesis (including detoxification of H2O2 derived from GULO), the physiological requirements for ascorbate and the ecological factors that determine the supply of dietary ascorbate throughout their life cycle.
source: The selective pressures resulting in GULO loss in animals represent a combination of the costs of ascorbate synthesis (including detoxification of H2O2 derived from GULO), the physiological requirements for ascorbate and the ecological factors that determine the supply of dietary ascorbate throughout their life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference about the factors influencing GULO loss in animals.

claim: The development of the photoprotective role of ascorbate in photosynthetic eukaryotes would have significantly altered its availability to many heterotrophic organisms.
source: The development of the photoprotective role of ascorbate in photosynthetic eukaryotes would have significantly altered its availability to many heterotrophic organisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the ecological consequences of ascorbate evolution.

claim: The leaves of land plants have particularly high cellular concentrations of ascorbate relative to other photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: The leaves of land plants have particularly high cellular concentrations of ascorbate relative to other photosynthetic eukaryotes (Gest et al., 2013), which may result from their inability to remove intracellular H2O2 via diffusion to an aquatic medium.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The high ascorbate concentration in land plant leaves may result from their inability to remove intracellular H2O2 via diffusion to an aquatic medium.
source: The leaves of land plants have particularly high cellular concentrations of ascorbate relative to other photosynthetic eukaryotes (Gest et al., 2013), which may result from their inability to remove intracellular H2O2 via diffusion to an aquatic medium.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: In almost all documented cases of ascorbate auxotrophy in animals, the major source of dietary ascorbate derives from GLDH rather than GULO.
source: Our dataset reveals that in almost all documented cases of ascorbate auxotrophy in animals, the major source of dietary ascorbate derives from GLDH rather than GULO (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of dietary sources shown in Table 1.

claim: The replacement of GULO with GLDH in photosynthetic organisms may have been an important contributory factor in the loss of GULO in many animal auxotrophs.
source: Thus, the replacement of GULO with GLDH in photosynthetic organisms may have ultimately been an important contributory factor in the loss of GULO in many animal auxotrophs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the dietary analysis.

source: Reverse transcriptase PCR was used to verify the expression of GULO in C. paradoxa (CCAP 981/1) and confirm its coding sequence.
evidence: This is a description of experimental methods.

claim: Arabidopsis vtc2 vtc5 double mutants lacking GDP-l-Gal phosphorylase activity are not viable unless supplemented with ascorbate.
source: For example, Arabidopsis vtc2 vtc5 double mutants lacking GDP-l-Gal phosphorylase activity are not viable unless supplemented with ascorbate, suggesting no other route can supply sufficient ascorbate to rescue this defect (Dowdle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The D-mannose/l-galactose pathway is the primary route of ascorbate biosynthesis in Arabidopsis.
source: Genetic evidence from a range of ascorbate-deficient Arabidopsis mutants indicates that the D-mannose/l-galactose pathway is the primary route of ascorbate biosynthesis (Conklin et al., 1999, 2006; Dowdle et al., 2007; Smirnoff, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
